claim: The sauropod hind limb was the main support that allowed their gigantic body masses.
source: The sauropod hind limb was the main support that allowed their gigantic body masses and a wide range of dynamic stability adaptations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational claim about sauropod anatomy.

claim: Deeply branched macronarians achieved increasingly arched hind limbs in what is known as wide-gauge posture.
source: Deeply branched macronarians achieved increasingly arched hind limbs in what is known as wide-gauge posture.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Some titanosaurians were the largest terrestrial vertebrates that ever existed.
source: However, it is not clear if this evolutionary trend is related to the evolutionary cascade toward gigantism even though some titanosaurians were the largest terrestrial vertebrates that ever existed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The macronarian hind limb becomes progressively more arched toward deeply branched groups, specifically Saltasauridae.
source: The macronarian hind limb does become progressively more arched toward deeply branched groups, specifically Saltasauridae.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the 3D geometric morphometric analysis.

claim: There is morphological convergence between different macronarian subclades.
source: However, there is morphological convergence between different macronarian subclades.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the morphometric analysis.

claim: Wide-gauge posture does not correlate with changes in body size deeper in the macronarian evolutionary tree.
source: Wide-gauge posture does not correlate with changes in body size deeper in the macronarian evolutionary tree and acted as an exaptation to gigantism.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on the analysis of evolutionary trends.

claim: Wide-gauge posture acted as an exaptation to gigantism.
source: Wide-gauge posture does not correlate with changes in body size deeper in the macronarian evolutionary tree and acted as an exaptation to gigantism.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract based on the lack of correlation between posture and body size.

claim: There is not a statistically significant trend toward a particular body size in titanosaurian subclades.
source: Despite some titanosaurian subclades becoming some of the largest vertebrates, there is not a statistically significant trend toward a particular body size, but we identify a phyletic body size decrease in Macronaria.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on statistical analysis.

claim: There is a phyletic body size decrease in Macronaria.
source: Despite some titanosaurian subclades becoming some of the largest vertebrates, there is not a statistically significant trend toward a particular body size, but we identify a phyletic body size decrease in Macronaria.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Sauropod dinosaurs reached some of the largest body masses of terrestrial vertebrates by one order of magnitude compared to other vertebrates.
source: Sauropod dinosaurs evolved a distinct body plan that allowed them to reach some of the largest body masses of terrestrial vertebrates (e.g. Bonaparte and Coria, 1993; Carballido et al., 2017; Lacovara et al., 2014; Sander, 2013; Sander et al., 2011a) by one order of magnitude compared to other vertebrates, including other megaherbivore dinosaurs (e.g. Maher et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Sauropods were dominant herbivorous dinosaurs throughout much of the Mesozoic.
source: Sauropods were dominant herbivorous dinosaurs throughout much of the Mesozoic (Sander, 2013; Sander et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Vertebral pneumaticity is related to avian-like air sacs in sauropods.
source: Several morphological features can be related to the evolutionary cascade that allowed the acquisition of their colossal sizes, such as the vertebral pneumaticity related to avian-like air sacs, high metabolic rates, cranial morphology, and feeding mechanisms (including the characteristic long necks among several other traits, see Sander, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The mechanical stability of columnar limbs allowed sauropods to support their multi-ton body masses.
source: The mechanical stability of the columnar limbs allowed them to support their multi-ton body masses (Bates et al., 2016; Lefebvre et al., 2022; Salgado et al., 1997; Sander, 2013; Ullmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There was an important evolutionary trend in the appendicular skeleton toward the acquisition of a stable limb posture known as wide-gauge.
source: Previous studies based on sauropod anatomical description, systematics, traditional morphometrics, biomechanics, and GMM suggested that there was an important evolutionary trend in the appendicular skeleton toward the acquisition of a stable limb posture known as wide-gauge (Klinkhamer et al., 2019; Lefebvre et al., 2022; Salgado et al., 1997; Sander, 2013; Ullmann et al., 2017; Upchurch et al., 2004; Voegele et al., 2021; Wilson and Carrano, 1999; Wilson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Wide-gauge posture appears among deeply branched Neosauropoda, in particular, among titanosauriforms.
source: This feature appears among deeply branched Neosauropoda, in particular, among titanosauriforms, which exhibit a progressively arched limb posture (Salgado et al., 1997; Upchurch et al., 2004; Voegele et al., 2021; Wilson and Carrano, 1999; Wilson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The wide stance may enable enhanced lateral stability during locomotion.
source: The wide stance may enable enhanced lateral stability during locomotion, allowing them to exploit more efficiently inland environments (Mannion and Upchurch, 2010; Ullmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations as a hypothesis.

claim: The widening of the body in Titanosauriformes and the acquisition of the wide-gauge stance is still poorly understood.
source: However, the widening of the body in Titanosauriformes and the acquisition of the wide-gauge stance is still poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: Arched limbs and wider postures appeared in the largest sauropods among Titanosauriformes.
source: Although the arched limbs and wider postures appeared in the largest sauropods among Titanosauriformes (Bates et al., 2016; Henderson, 2006; Ullmann et al., 2017; Wilson and Carrano, 1999), these features may at least be acquired independently among both small and large titanosauriforms of different subclades (Henderson, 2006; Bates et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Arched limbs and wider postures may be acquired independently among both small and large titanosauriforms of different subclades.
source: Although the arched limbs and wider postures appeared in the largest sauropods among Titanosauriformes (Bates et al., 2016; Henderson, 2006; Ullmann et al., 2017; Wilson and Carrano, 1999), these features may at least be acquired independently among both small and large titanosauriforms of different subclades (Henderson, 2006; Bates et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Limb posture may have been related to achieving greater ranges of ecological niches through biomechanical stability rather than allowing increasing their body size itself.
source: Limb posture may have been related to achieving greater ranges of ecological niches through biomechanical stability rather than allowing increasing their body size itself (e.g. Bates et al., 2016; Henderson, 2006; Ullmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations as a hypothesis.

claim: The size of the femur and tibia correlates well with sauropod body mass.
source: We chose the centroid size of the hind limb because the size of the femur and tibia correlates well with sauropod body mass (Campione and Evans, 2020; Mazzetta et al., 2004), but alternative tests using femoral length or body mass estimations are provided in Appendix 1-2 and Supplementary file 2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A total of 16 shape Principal Components were obtained after Anderson's χ test.
source: A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed to generate an occupation morphospace, obtaining a total of 16 shape Principal Components (after Anderson's χ test; PCs from now on).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the PCA analysis.

claim: The first six PCs accounted for 78.3% of the cumulative morphological variation.
source: The first six PCs accounted for 78.3% of the cumulative morphological variation (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Table 2.

claim: No single shape variable reports significant differences among sauropod subclades according to the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test.
source: The non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test shows that no single shape variable reports significant differences among sauropod subclades (Tables 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Tables 3 and 4.

claim: Non-titanosaurian macronarians occupy negative values in PC1.
source: Non-titanosaurian macronarians occupy negative values, whereas non-lithostrotian titanosaurs are distributed between weakly negative (e.g. Bonatitan) and positive PC1 values (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing PC1 distribution.

claim: The highest positive PC1 values are occupied by saltasaurids (i.e. Saltasaurus and Neuquensaurus).
source: The highest positive PC1 values are occupied by saltasaurids (i.e. Saltasaurus and Neuquensaurus; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing PC1 distribution.

claim: PC2 summarizes 14.83% of the variance.
source: PC2 (summarizing 14.83% of the variance; Figure 3a–b) is associated with characters describing the orientation of the femoral shaft; the length and orientation of the femur proximal end; the length, width, and orientation of the distal femoral condyles; the orientation of the tibial shaft; the length and orientation of the cnemial crest; the length, width, and orientation of the tibial distal end; the orientation of the tibial ascending process; the orientation of the fibular shaft and fibular anterior crest (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing PC2.

claim: There is no clear pattern among the titanosaurian subclade morphospace or phylomorphospace among progressively deeply branching titanosauriforms in PC2.
source: However, there is no clear pattern among the titanosaurian subclade morphospace (Figure 3a) or the phylomorphospace (Figure 3b) among progressively deeply branching titanosauriforms.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing PC2 distribution.

claim: PC3 summarizes 11.61% of the variance.
source: Finally, PC3 (summarizing 11.61% of the variance; Figures 3a–b–4a–b) is related to characters describing the orientation of the femoral shaft and head; the length of the femoral lateral bulge; the location and orientation of the fourth trochanter; the orientation of the distal femoral condyles; the length and orientation of the tibial cnemial crest; the length of the tibial distal end; the length of the tibial ascending process; and the length and morphology of the fibula (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing PC3.

claim: There is a trend from positive values to negative values of PC3 from more basally branching titanosauriforms to more deeply nested ones.
source: In the phylomorphospace, there is a trend from positive values to negative values of PC3 (Figure 4b) from more basally branching titanosauriforms to more deeply nested ones.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing PC3 distribution.

claim: There is a trend in hind limb centroid size distribution from large, non-titanosaurian macronarians in the Early Cretaceous to small, deeply nested lithostrotian titanosaurs in the Late Cretaceous.
source: There is a trend in hind limb centroid size distribution from large, non-titanosaurian macronarians in the Early Cretaceous (e.g. Euhelopus) to small, deeply nested lithostrotian titanosaurs in the Late Cretaceous (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing size distribution.

claim: The RMA models found no significant correlation between the shape variables and the log-transformed centroid size.
source: However, the RMA models found no significant correlation between the shape variables and the log-transformed centroid size (Table 5, see Figure 6 and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing RMA analysis.

claim: The PC1 model found negative allometry but no significant correlation (r2=0.105, p-value = 0.204).
source: The PC1 model (r2=0.105, p-value = 0.204; Figure 6a) found negative allometry but no significant correlation and the percentage of variance explained by hind limb size differences was small.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing RMA analysis with specific statistical values.

claim: Pagel's lambda estimation shows a significant phylogenetic signal in log-transformed hind limb centroid size (λ=0.982).
source: Pagel's lambda (λ) estimation shows a significant phylogenetic signal in log-transformed hind limb centroid size (λ=0.982), and PC1 (λ=0.715), PC3 (λ=0.760), PC5 (λ=0.778) and PC6 (λ=0.697) therefore exhibiting a trend in the evolution of Titanosauriformes (Table 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing phylogenetic signal analysis.

claim: PC1 shows a significant phylogenetic signal (λ=0.715).
source: Pagel's lambda (λ) estimation shows a significant phylogenetic signal in log-transformed hind limb centroid size (λ=0.982), and PC1 (λ=0.715), PC3 (λ=0.760), PC5 (λ=0.778) and PC6 (λ=0.697) therefore exhibiting a trend in the evolution of Titanosauriformes (Table 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing phylogenetic signal analysis.

claim: PC3 shows a significant phylogenetic signal (λ=0.760).
source: Pagel's lambda (λ) estimation shows a significant phylogenetic signal in log-transformed hind limb centroid size (λ=0.982), and PC1 (λ=0.715), PC3 (λ=0.760), PC5 (λ=0.778) and PC6 (λ=0.697) therefore exhibiting a trend in the evolution of Titanosauriformes (Table 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing phylogenetic signal analysis.

claim: Tests recover significant trends toward a decrease in hind limb size across all titanosauriform subclades.
source: The resulting tests recover significant trends toward a decrease in hind limb size across all titanosauriform subclades, with positive PC1 values including somphospondyli titanosauriformes, and negative PC3 values across all titanosauriform subclades (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing evolutionary trends.

claim: The evolutionary pattern observed for the titanosaurian hind limb may be explained by convergent evolution.
source: Based on the lack of significant phylogenetic differences and the presence of morphological similarities, the evolutionary pattern observed for the titanosaurian hind limb may be explained by convergent evolution, consistent with previous analyses (Lefebvre et al., 2022; Páramo, 2020; Ullmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The acquisition of wide-gauge locomotion would be the main source of hind limb morphological variability in titanosaurian sauropods.
source: Considering the analyzed sample, the acquisition of wide-gauge locomotion would be the main source of hind limb morphological variability in titanosaurian sauropods (Figures 2 and 5) and possesses a significant phylogenetic signal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The trend toward a more arched limb posture persists in the more deeply nested titanosaurs.
source: The trend toward a more arched limb posture persists in the more deeply nested titanosaurs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the results.

claim: Oceanotitan dantasi exhibits a columnar hind limb characterized by no deflection of the femoral head with regard to the tibial condyle.
source: Oceanotitan dantasi, a possible representative of Somphospondyli, exhibits a columnar hind limb characterized by no deflection of the femoral head with regard to the tibial condyle (although some titanosauriforms exhibit this feature, see Royo-Torres, 2009; recent phylogenetic approaches suggest that O. dantasi might represent non-titanosauriform macronarian, see Mocho et al., 2024a), and a straight and long, lateromedially narrow zeugopod with few anterior rotations of the fibula (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing specific taxa.

claim: The acquisition of robust and arched hind limbs was previously proposed as a trend in Titanosauria.
source: In general, the results obtained here confirm the previously proposed trend toward the acquisition of robust and arched hind limbs in Titanosauria (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section confirming previous hypotheses.

claim: Once hind limb mechanical stability was acquired, the increasingly arched and robust morphologies established within Titanosauria cannot be fully related to an increase in body mass.
source: Nevertheless, once hind limb mechanical stability was acquired (following e.g. Ullmann et al., 2017) the increasingly arched and robust morphologies established within Titanosauria cannot be fully related to an increase in body mass (Figure 6a) and are better explained as convergence between different subclades (Figures 2 and 6, see evolutionary trend breakdown in Table 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a primary conclusion.

claim: The progressively arched limb was probably hard-coded in the macronarian bauplan.
source: This progressively arched limb was probably hard-coded in the macronarian bauplan and, after the somphospondylan stable posture was acquired, was still present but relatable to a significant variability of biomechanical adaptations (Voegele et al., 2021) as our analyses suggest.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: Morphological differences in the fore limb elongation in sauropods may be related to different feeding niche capabilities.
source: Despite the biomechanical diversity associated with hind limb morphology being still unclear, several studies point out that morphological differences in the fore limb elongation in sauropods may be related to different feeding niche capabilities (Bates et al., 2016; Upchurch et al., 2021; Vidal et al., 2020; Voegele et al., 2020), including discussion on possible bipedal/tripodial rearing abilities that are much more developed, particularly in sauropods with a hyper-robust hind limb (Upchurch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Dreadnoughtus exhibits a hyper-robust hind limb with subequal autopodial lengths and a wedged sacrum.
source: Interestingly, Dreadnoughtus exhibits this hyper-robust hind limb with subequal autopodial lengths and a wedged sacrum (Vidal et al., 2020; Voegele et al., 2021), an anteriorly placed body Centre of Masses (CoM; Bates et al., 2016) and possibly high browsing feeding capabilities (e.g. Vidal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The acquisition of a hyper-robust and arched hind limb morphology is possibly related to improved skeletal support in high browsing and extremely large sauropods.
source: It is possible that the acquisition of a hyper-robust and arched hind limb morphology is related to improved skeletal support in high browsing and extremely large sauropods like Dreadnoughtus, which in combination with their size and neck dorsiflexion capabilities (e.g. Vidal et al., 2020) allowed them to feed in a high niche stratification, independent of the acquisition of rearing capabilities.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: PC2 does not provide a phylogenetic signal for the titanosaurian evolution.
source: Although PC2 does not provide a phylogenetic signal for the titanosaurian evolution, it reveals significant differences among smaller titanosaurian taxa with robust hind limbs and especially hyper-robust zeugopodia (Figure 3), like Magyarosaurus and the saltasaurines Neuquensaurus and Saltasaurus, which can be related to different roles in the necessary mechanical stability for rearing capabilities (following Upchurch et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing PC2 results.

claim: The differences among robust hind limb titanosaurian morphologies may suggest that their convergence is due to different biomechanical adaptations.
source: The differences among robust hind limb titanosaurian morphologies may suggest that their convergence is due to other sources of variation (i.e. different biomechanical adaptations).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation.

claim: All lithostrotian titanosaurs that exhibit a slightly rotated fibula and extremely arched hind limb morphology independent of their size exhibit femora with reduced fibular epicondyles.
source: It is also important to note that all the lithostrotian titanosaurs that exhibit a slightly rotated fibula, whether sigmoid or not, and extremely arched hind limb morphology independent of their size, exhibit femora with reduced fibular epicondyles (after Otero et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation with a citation.

claim: The hind limb of Muyelensaurus and Mendozasaurus exhibits a distinctive plotting, often overlapping with Aeolosaurus.
source: Here, we found a distinctive plotting for the rinconsaurian hind limb of Muyelensaurus and Mendozasaurus, often overlapping with Aeolosaurus, as in the PC1 and PC3 morphospaces (Figures 2—4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing specific taxa.

claim: Some lithostrotians shift away from the main early-branching lithostrotian area of the morphospace towards a straighter, elongated hind limb convergent with non-titanosaurian macronarians.
source: In addition, the phylomorphospaces indicate that some lithostrotians shift away from the main early-branching lithostrotian area of the morphospace towards a straighter, elongated hind limb convergent with non-titanosaurian macronarians (Figures 2a–b–4a–b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing morphospace occupation.

claim: Colossosauria includes several of the largest titanosaurs ever known.
source: Colossosauria includes several of the largest titanosaurs ever known (Carballido et al., 2017; Riga et al., 2019) as well as some of the smallest lithostrotian titanosaurs in South America that are placed within Rinconsauria, which has been recently recovered as an early branching lineage of Colossosauria (Carballido et al., 2017; Riga et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Colossosauria includes some of the smallest lithostrotian titanosaurs in South America that are placed within Rinconsauria.
source: Colossosauria includes several of the largest titanosaurs ever known (Carballido et al., 2017; Riga et al., 2019) as well as some of the smallest lithostrotian titanosaurs in South America that are placed within Rinconsauria, which has been recently recovered as an early branching lineage of Colossosauria (Carballido et al., 2017; Riga et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: There is a trend in the evolution of titanosaurs towards a decrease in size.
source: Our results with the current time-calibrated supertree topology indicate that there is a trend in the evolution of titanosaurs towards a decrease in size (Figures 5 and 7, Tables 5–6).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a primary finding.

claim: Lithostrotians may not follow Cope's rule.
source: In the light of our current sample, once many of the hind limb features relatable to wide-gauge posture are acquired, there is a phylogenetical trend, close to a pure Brownian motion model, toward an overall decreasing size (log-transformed hind limb centroid size λ=0.982), which is consistent with previous results that indicated that lithostrotians (or even all macronarian sauropods) may not follow Cope's rule (Carrano, 2006; de Souza and Santucci, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Within Titanosauria, the hind limb arched morphology does not correspond to the significant trend toward a size decrease observed in this sauropod clade.
source: Within Titanosauria, the hind limb arched morphology (increasing wide-gauge posture) does not correspond to the significant trend toward a size decrease observed in this sauropod clade (see Figure 7, Tables 6–7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a primary finding.

claim: Large titanosaurs show very different hind limb morphologies.
source: Large titanosaurs show very different hind limb morphologies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: Most of the lithostrotians that exhibit extremely arched hind limbs, robust elements, and reduced zeugopod elements decrease in size.
source: In this context, it is remarkable that most of the lithostrotians that exhibit extremely arched hind limbs, robust elements, and reduced zeugopod elements decrease in size, like Saltasaurus or Magyarosaurus (Figure 2, see discussion on morphological convergence above).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: The trend toward arched hind limbs breaks in titanosaurian sauropods, with more variable morphologies and large overlapping of morphospaces.
source: Our test found that the trend toward this type of hind limb breaks in titanosaurian sauropods, with more variable morphologies and large overlapping of morphospaces, whereas the hind limb size decreases (Figure 7, Tables 6–7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a primary finding.

claim: PC1-PC3 exhibits some of the morphological features that are classically related to wide-gauge arching morphology.
source: Most importantly, PC1-PC3 exhibits some of the morphological features that are classically related to wide-gauge arching morphology (e.g.) and our analyses found a significant trend toward increasingly arched hind limbs (Tables 8 and 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing PC results.

claim: The analyses found a significant trend toward increasingly arched hind limbs.
source: Most importantly, PC1-PC3 exhibits some of the morphological features that are classically related to wide-gauge arching morphology (e.g.) and our analyses found a significant trend toward increasingly arched hind limbs (Tables 8 and 9).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a primary finding.

claim: Post-Cenomanian lithostrotians exhibit great morphological variability.
source: However, the post-Cenomanian lithostrotians exhibit great morphological variability, with several taxa exhibiting plesiomorphic columnar femora (i.e. Ampelosaurus, Aeolosaurus, Magyarosaurus) and slightly straight zeugopodial elements, with anteriorly expanded tibial proximal ends, and straight non-rotated fibula expanded in the anterior view (Figures 4 and 7; see discussion on morphological convergence above).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: The large size variability in the post-early Coniacian cannot be related to the morphological features that are classically associated with the progressively arched morphology.
source: Similarly, the large size variability in the post-early Coniacian cannot be related to the morphological features that are classically associated with the progressively arched morphology (Figure 7), as discussed before.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: Rapetosaurus is based on juvenile and subadult specimens.
source: Notice that Rapetosaurus is based on juvenile and subadult specimens, and it may retain a plesiomorphic slender morphology that changes in the adult (see precocial development in the limbs of Rapetosaurus) (Curry Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The main features related to the acquisition of an arched hind limb posture are typical of more deeply nested titanosaurs such as saltasaurines.
source: Our results suggest that the main features related to the acquisition of an arched hind limb posture (presence of lateromedially wide femora with robust zeugopods) are typical of more deeply nested titanosaurs such as saltasaurines (Carrano, 2005; Lefebvre et al., 2022; Sander et al., 2011a; Ullmann et al., 2017; Vila et al., 2022; Wilson and Carrano, 1999) and exhibit a significant phylogenetic signal about titanosaurian evolution (Table 5, Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section with supporting citations.

claim: The arched morphology usually related to wide-gauge posture is an exaptation initially related to increasing body size.
source: The arched morphology usually related to wide-gauge posture is an exaptation initially related to increasing body size.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a primary conclusion.

claim: Once fully acquired within Somphospondyli, arched posture features are no longer related to increasing body size.
source: However, once fully acquired within Somphospondyli, these features are no longer related to increasing body size, as increases in the arched posture and the development of hyper-robust zeugopods are features that evolved independently in several lineages and are shared by several of both the smallest and largest taxa in different titanosaurian lineages (Figure 6, Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a primary conclusion.

claim: There is an evolutionary trend toward decreasing titanosaurian hind limb size based on the size of the hind limb centroid.
source: Also, there is an evolutionary trend toward decreasing titanosaurian hind limb size (and body size; Figure 7), based on the size of the hind limb centroid.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a primary finding.

claim: The lack of correlation between the arched posture and body size may be related to a wide morphological variation within Lithostrotia.
source: The lack of correlation between the arched posture, position, and robustness of zeugopod, among other traits with the body size, may also be related to a wide morphological variation within Lithostrotia (Figures 2—4).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an interpretation.

claim: There is a large morphological convergence between the different titanosaurian subclades.
source: It can be noted that, together with a trend toward increasingly arched hind limbs and reduced zeugopods with increasingly rotated fibulae, there is also a large morphological convergence between the different titanosaurian subclades, as indicated by both our non-phylogenetic and phylogenetic analyses (Tables 2–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a primary finding.

claim: Large morphological convergences unrelated to body size may be a response to different morphofunctional adaptations.
source: Large morphological convergences unrelated to body size may be a response to different morphofunctional adaptations.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an interpretation.

claim: The convergences in hind limb morphology of titanosaurs may explain biomechanical similarities.
source: The convergences in hind limb morphology of titanosaurs may explain biomechanical similarities.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as an interpretation.

claim: 17 macronarian sauropod hind limbs were 3D-digitized and analyzed using 3D Geometric Morphometrics.
source: To analyze the morphology, 17 macronarian sauropod hind limbs (Table 1) were 3D-digitized and analyzed using 3D Geometric Morphometrics tool-kit (3D-GMM; Gunz et al., 2005; Páramo, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the sample.

claim: A total of 28 landmarks and 12 semilandmark curves were placed on the hind limb bones.
source: A total of 28 landmarks and 12 semilandmark curves were placed on the hind limb bones partly based on previous studies (Lefebvre et al., 2022; Páramo et al., 2020; Páramo, 2020; Table 2, Figure 2, Supplementary file 1) using IDAV Landmark Editor software (Wiley et al., 2005; dataset with the landmark and semilandmark curves coordinates can be accessed in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the landmark placement.

claim: The MRP-supertree methodology was used to estimate a consensus tree topology.
source: Evolutionary trend analyses were accomplished after the estimation of a consensus tree topology using the MRP-supertree methodology (Bininda-Emonds, 2004) with the phangorn package (Schliep et al., 2017; Schliep, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Sauropod body mass was proxied by hind limb centroid size collected from the GPA.
source: Sauropod body mass was proxied by hind limb centroid size collected from the GPA.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing size measurement.

claim: The hind limb is the main sauropod body mass support.
source: However, as the hind limb is the main sauropod body mass support, it can be better used as a 'conservative-minimal' approach to its body mass, with larger hind limb corresponding to giant titanosaurian taxa.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section as justification for the proxy.

claim: Reduced Major Axis (RMA) regression was used to test for allometric relationships between sauropod hind limb shape variables and centroid size.
source: We tested for allometric relationships between the sauropod hind limb shape variables (PCs) and the centroid size as proxy to body mass via Reduced Major Axis (RMA) regression using lmodel2 R package (Legendre, 2018); but an alternative set of analyses was carried out using femoral length and body mass estimations (see Supplementary file 2 and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing statistical analysis.

claim: Pagel's lambda was used to test for the phylogenetic signal of shape variables and hind limb centroid size.
source: We used the time-calibrated supertree topology and our shape variables (PCs) and hind limb centroid size to generate the Pagel's lambda (λ) with the 'phytools' R package and test for the phylogenetic signal of these traits.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing phylogenetic signal analysis.

claim: Ancestral characters were estimated using maximum-likelihood and a simple Brownian evolutionary model.
source: Once those PCs that exhibit significant phylogenetic signal were identified, as well as the log-transformed centroid size, we estimated their ancestral characters (ACEs) using maximum-likelihood and a simple Brownian evolutionary model similar to the one assumed for estimation of Pagel's lambda.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing ancestral character estimation.

claim: A χ2 goodness-of-fit test was used to evaluate whether body size is increasing or decreasing over titanosaurian evolution.
source: We used a χ2 goodness-of-fit test to evaluate whether body size is increasing or decreasing, and shape-PCs occur at the same frequency (50–50% null hypothesis) or have a positive or negative tendency over titanosaurian evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing statistical testing.

claim: Oceanotitan dantasi is a possible member of Somphospondyli.
source: Both the early branching macronarian Oceanotitan - a possible member of Somphospondyli (Mocho et al., 2019b) - and the euhelopodid somphospondyli Euhelopus occupy positive and negative values near a zero score, whereas the early-diverging somphospondylan Ligabuesaurus is distributed at slightly more positive PC2 values than Oceanotitan (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Lohuecotitan has been recovered as a member of Lithostrotia in recent phylogenetic analyses.
source: In this PC1, the Titanosauria node splits near a zero score, with Lohuecotitan occupying weakly positive PC1 values near a zero score [in recent phylogenetic analyses, Lohuecotitan has been recovered as a member of Lithostrotia (Díez Díaz et al., 2021a; Navarro et al., 2022; Mocho et al., 2024b)], but other deeply nested titanosaurs occupy positive scores in PC1 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Lirainosaurinae was not recovered as a monophyletic group in the current topology.
source: However, both Colossosauria and the two analyzed members of Lirainosaurinae fall into negative PC1 values (Lirainosaurinae was not recovered as a monophyletic group in our current topology Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing phylogenetic results.

claim: The Mann-Whitney U test found no significant differences in PC2 in any of the pairwise comparisons.
source: The Mann-Whitney U test found no significant differences in the PC2 in any of the pairwise comparisons (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing statistical test results.

claim: The pair-wise Mann-Whitney U test found no significant differences between sauropod subclades in PC3.
source: The pair-wise Mann-Whitney U test found no significant differences between sauropod subclades in this PC (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing statistical test results.

claim: The smallest lithostrotians are concentrated at deeply branching nodes, including the Ibero-Armorican lirainosaurines, Bonatitan reigi, Magyarosaurus spp. and members of Saltasaurinae.
source: The smallest lithostrotians are concentrated at deeply branching nodes, including the Ibero-Armorican lirainosaurines, Bonatitan reigi, Magyarosaurus spp. and members of Saltasaurinae (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing size distribution.

claim: Almost all of the RMA models found a negative relationship between shape variables and log-transformed centroid size.
source: Almost all of the RMA found a negative relationship, except for several sub-sampled RMA models like the PC2 against log-transformed centroid size for the sample of lithostrotian titanosaurs only (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing RMA results.

claim: None of the RMA models for the sub-samples found a significant correlation.
source: None of the RMA models for the sub-samples found a significant correlation (see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing RMA results.

claim: Titanosaurian sauropods appeared unambiguously during the Early Cretaceous.
source: Titanosaurian sauropods appeared unambiguously during the Early Cretaceous (D'emic, 2012; Mannion et al., 2019b; Poropat et al., 2016) just as lithostrotian titanosaurs appeared early after the Valanginian-Hauterivian (Mannion et al., 2019b; Poropat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Lithostrotian titanosaurs appeared early after the Valanginian-Hauterivian.
source: Titanosaurian sauropods appeared unambiguously during the Early Cretaceous (D'emic, 2012; Mannion et al., 2019b; Poropat et al., 2016) just as lithostrotian titanosaurs appeared early after the Valanginian-Hauterivian (Mannion et al., 2019b; Poropat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The colossosaurian node may have branched in the early Albian according to several recent phylogenetic hypotheses.
source: Considering several recent phylogenetic hypotheses, the colossosaurian node may have branched in the early Albian (Gorscak et al., 2022; Sallam et al., 2018; Vila et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Saltasaurid lithostrotians are traced back to the late Albian in recent studies.
source: Saltasaurid lithostrotians are nevertheless traced back to the late Albian in recent studies (Sallam et al., 2018; Vila et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Atsinganosaurus was recently recovered as a member of Lirainosaurinae.
source: Atsinganosaurus, an Ibero-Armorican lithostrotian, was recently recovered as a member of Lirainosaurinae (; Díez Díaz et al., 2018, Mocho et al., 2024b) or as a lognkosaurian colossosaur (Gorscak and O'Connor, 2019; Vila et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Atsinganosaurus was recovered as a lognkosaurian colossosaur in some phylogenetic analyses.
source: Atsinganosaurus, an Ibero-Armorican lithostrotian, was recently recovered as a member of Lirainosaurinae (; Díez Díaz et al., 2018, Mocho et al., 2024b) or as a lognkosaurian colossosaur (Gorscak and O'Connor, 2019; Vila et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Each element of the hind limb is separated by an articular cap much larger than in other known extant archosaurs.
source: Each element of the hind limb is separated by an articular cap much larger than in other known extant archosaurs (Bonnan et al., 2013; Holliday et al., 2010; Schwarz et al., 2007; Voegele et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.

claim: The femur may exhibit the best correlation between cartilage cap and bone morphology constrained by its role as support under most of the stress of the body mass.
source: The femur, and the hind limb overall, may exhibit the best correlation between cartilage cap and bone morphology constrained by its role as support under most of the stress of the body mass (Bonnan et al., 2013; Voegele et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section with supporting citations.
